# The Early Access Playbook ([.md](https://dub.sh/earlyaccessplaybook-md))

*Build with real people. Learn faster. Keep improving until your product delivers its promise.*

By **[Hiten Shah](https://www.hiten.com/)** [**(X)**](https://x.com/hnshah)

At [KISSmetrics](https://producthabits.com/my-billion-dollar-mistake/), we spent roughly eighteen months on two product directions that missed the mark. One attracted Facebook application developers who couldn't pay. The next required too much work before customers saw value. I wish we'd spent more of that time learning how people were already solving the problems we wanted to fix.

Today AI can turn an idea into working software in hours. Teams can ship another version before learning what happened with the last one. I wrote this playbook to help founders and product teams learn while there's still room to change what they're building.

**The faster you can build, the faster you need to learn.**

Early access is where I want that learning to happen.

## What early access actually means

Early access starts with a few people who already have the problem you want to solve. You can find them before writing code. Ask about the last time they tried to do the job, what they used and where the work got difficult. When there's a product to try, invite them to use it for something real.

A job is something a person already needs to get done. Before a meeting, for example, someone may need a document buried in several apps. They might search folders or ask a coworker. You need to understand that existing method before you can tell whether your product makes it better.

Watch what happens when someone tries the real task. Notice where they get stuck and what help they need. Make a change worth testing, then invite them back. The relationship gives participants a way to shape something useful and gives your team evidence for the next decision.

## Two ways to use this playbook

**Building something new?** Find people who already do the job. You can start with conversations, a manual service or a working first version. Learn whether the problem matters before treating your solution as settled.

**Adding a feature?** Start with customers' existing habits. Define the current task and how well they complete it. Give a few eligible customers deliberate access to the change and compare their experience with the old way. Preserve the original workflow and a way to roll back if needed.

Both paths use the same six plays. If you already know the job and the people, go straight to [Play 04](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1bo9n52j_M4Nx094TObZQVAq1htlB6h9XlySLgFsH710/edit?tab=t.7dlrt9su90ms) and watch real work. When usage has exposed an important failure, start at [Play 05](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1bo9n52j_M4Nx094TObZQVAq1htlB6h9XlySLgFsH710/edit?tab=t.l768kjlu84i5). The right starting point is the decision you're trying to make.

## The ideas that shaped how I build products

Eric Ries popularized Build–Measure–Learn through [The Lean Startup](https://leanstartup.co/about/principles/). When I was at KISSmetrics, I wanted us to design a visual that would make the methodology easier to understand. We created the diagram below, built around three phrases that still hold up today.

![Diagram of the Lean Startup Build–Measure–Learn cycle, connecting ideas, building, code, measurement, data and learning, with practices for accelerating each stage.][image1]

*The Lean Startup methodology, created by Eric Ries. Original illustration designed by KISSmetrics.*

**Build faster. Measure faster. Learn faster.**

The diagram helped us see product development as a cycle of assumptions, tests and learning. Customer interviews and usability tests sat alongside cohort analysis and continuous deployment. It reminded us that shipping was a means of learning.

AI has changed how quickly we can build. It has also made it easier to act on another assumption before examining the last one. The learning part of the loop deserves more attention.

### Steve Blank is revisiting the methodology too

Steve Blank helped establish the idea that founders should test their assumptions with customers. In September 2026, he revisited his [Lean LaunchPad](https://steveblank.com/2026/09/30/lean-launchpad-the-next-generation/) curriculum for an era when AI makes it possible to build convincing software quickly.

In [*AI Killed the MVP — Long Live the IUP*](https://steveblank.com/2026/09/25/ai-killed-the-mvp-long-live-the-iup/), Blank calls the new risk an Initial Untested Product. Something can appear finished before anyone has established whether people need it. A polished interface can hide a weak customer assumption.

Blank emphasizes customer discovery and real commitments from design partners. Someone who volunteers time or lets you examine a workflow gives you more to investigate than someone who says an idea sounds promising. You still have to watch whether the product helps.

Synthetic interviews can help prepare questions. They can't establish what a customer did. Blank checks generated research against interviews with people, and I think that's the right boundary.

You can generate a hundred plausible customer conversations without learning what anyone will do with your product. Seeing a real person try a real task remains a useful check.

## What if talking to customers makes your product worse?

Keith Rabois argued on [Lenny's Podcast](https://www.lennysnewsletter.com/p/hard-truths-about-building-in-the-ai-era/) in April 2026 that customer interviews can harm consumer and small-business products. I take the objection seriously. People can be enthusiastic about an idea and never use the product. They can also be wrong about why they make decisions.

Fifty interviews can produce a convincing story and still point you toward the wrong product. The question is what a conversation lets you reasonably conclude and what you must observe next.

### The problem with asking people what they want

Customer research can mislead you in several ways. These are the mistakes I would watch for most closely.

* **Feature requests become the roadmap.** You collect suggestions and build things that don't solve a meaningful problem.  
* **Enthusiasm gets mistaken for demand.** People say they'd use something but never change what they're already doing.  
* **Repeated complaints look like market evidence.** Several people describe the same problem, but they all belong to one narrow group.  
* **One successful task becomes proof of a business.** Someone completes something once, and you assume you've discovered repeatable value.

In each case, the conclusion outruns the evidence. Rabois' criticism is an important reminder that a founder has to decide what can reasonably be inferred from an interview, a request or a successful task.

### Start with things that actually happened

I prefer asking people about specific experiences. A useful starting question is, "Tell me about the last time you tried to do this." From there, I want to understand what happened first, which tools they used and where they struggled. That sequence gives me concrete actions to investigate. If someone struggled to find a document, I want to know what they were looking for, where they searched, what they remembered and how they eventually found it.

Even a detailed account can be inaccurate, so I look for an artifact or an opportunity to watch someone attempt the work. Once there's a product, the questions become more direct. Can they accomplish the job? Where do they hesitate? How much help do they need? What happens when that need arises again? Real attempts can reveal problems that nobody would think to mention in an interview.

Observation still requires judgment. A failed task could mean the interface is confusing, the necessary data is unavailable or the person falls outside the intended audience. The same result can support several explanations, which is why a useful test should lead to a specific next question rather than an automatic feature decision.

### What different kinds of evidence tell you

Not every signal establishes the same thing. An interview demonstrates willingness to talk, and a test demonstrates what happened in a particular situation. Repeated successful use and value for a new group are stronger evidence, but each still has limits.

| Evidence | What you learn | What remains unknown |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **Someone agrees to an interview** | They're willing to discuss the problem | Whether they need your solution |
| **Someone commits time to testing** | They're willing to invest effort | Whether the product delivers value |
| **Someone completes a real task** | The product can help in that situation | Whether they'll use it again |
| **Someone succeeds when the need recurs** | The product provides repeat value in observed situations | Whether the result extends to a larger market |
| **A new group experiences similar value** | The result may extend beyond the original participants | Whether adoption and economics support a business |

An early group can help you discover whether a product is becoming valuable. Its behavior alone cannot establish market-wide demand or retention, especially when the participants were deliberately selected and received unusual help.

### Founder judgment still matters

Customers can show you where a job breaks down. Their feature requests may point toward a solution, but deciding what to build remains the founder's job. Sometimes the request is wrong and the underlying problem is right.

Early access gives you a chance to test those judgments before they become expensive.

## What early access looked like at FYI

In 2017, Marie Prokopets and I started researching what became FYI, a product for finding and organizing work documents. We spent five hours writing a six-question survey about people's roles, companies, tools and challenges working with documents. One question asked openly about their biggest difficulty. We deliberately avoided explaining the product we planned to build because we didn't want our proposed solution shaping their answers.

The sixth question took a different approach.

**"How can you participate in helping us build this software?"**

People could volunteer for interviews, give feedback on screenshots or participate in future product tests. We shared the research through an email series with readers who already followed our work, then explained why we'd asked the questions. The survey received 653 responses. The research that followed included 52 interviews. Those numbers describe two distinct stages of research. Neither measures product adoption.

The survey helped identify people with relevant experience, and the interviews revealed more about their work and where it broke down. Later, we built a search-focused MVP in five days. Testing exposed an assumption we hadn't fully accounted for. Some people couldn't remember enough of a document's title or the right search terms, but they remembered the person associated with it or the activity surrounding it. That observation led us to explore finding documents through people and recent activity.

Actual product use influenced the direction of the solution. I can't tell you exactly how much the subsequent changes improved task completion or retention because the surviving historical records don't establish those results. The case still shows something useful about learning from real attempts. Research helped us understand the job. Watching people use the product challenged our first approach.

The sixth survey question mattered for another reason. It helped turn an initial research exchange into an opportunity to keep learning together as the product evolved. You don't need a newsletter audience or a six-question survey to do the same. You need a way to find relevant people, give them a worthwhile reason to participate and return to their work as the product changes.

[Read the original early-access survey approach](https://producthabits.com/early-access-surveys/). [Read Marie's account of the FYI research](https://www.userinterviews.com/blog/beta-testing-products-what-to-ask-and-why).

## How the playbook works {#how-the-playbook-works}

The six plays turn what you learn into a series of decisions. You can enter the cycle wherever your current product and evidence justify it.

| Play | What you do | What you leave with |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| [**01 Define the promise**](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1bo9n52j_M4Nx094TObZQVAq1htlB6h9XlySLgFsH710/edit?tab=t.cya3ughhip7h) | Choose the person, the job, and the valuable result. Understand what they do today. | Promise Card |
| [**02 Assemble the group**](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1bo9n52j_M4Nx094TObZQVAq1htlB6h9XlySLgFsH710/edit?tab=t.lbvo022518zk) | Find people who do that work. Invite them into a voluntary learning relationship. | Qualified cohort and Access Contract |
| [**03 Find the Pattern of Pain**](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1bo9n52j_M4Nx094TObZQVAq1htlB6h9XlySLgFsH710/edit?tab=t.ds8fxfwg51rl) | Investigate recent experiences, recurring problems, and counterexamples. | Episode Records and Pattern of Pain |
| [**04 Watch real work**](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1bo9n52j_M4Nx094TObZQVAq1htlB6h9XlySLgFsH710/edit?tab=t.7dlrt9su90ms) | Observe someone trying the job with your product, including assistance needed. | Observation Record |
| [**05 Improve and retest**](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1bo9n52j_M4Nx094TObZQVAq1htlB6h9XlySLgFsH710/edit?tab=t.l768kjlu84i5) | Choose a change, consider other explanations, and test the result. | Decision Receipt and retest plan |
| [**06 Prove value and decide**](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1bo9n52j_M4Nx094TObZQVAq1htlB6h9XlySLgFsH710/edit?tab=t.reojhvytzs5q) | Examine who received value and whether another group can experience it too. | Value and Cohort Review |

The [field kit in Tab 07](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1bo9n52j_M4Nx094TObZQVAq1htlB6h9XlySLgFsH710/edit?tab=t.3bzsn4yoxak2) contains completed examples and blank forms. The plays don't always move in a straight line. A failed task might suggest a product change, or it could make you question whether you're solving the right problem. **You finish a play when you have enough evidence to make its decision.** Completing a worksheet alone isn't the goal.

Choose your starting point based on where you are today.

* **Exploring a new idea?** Define the promise and learn from people who already do the job.  
* **Have a working product?** Watch someone attempt a real task.  
* **Already working with early users?** Start with the decision their experiences have created.

## Run your first learning cycle

Choose one product decision. You might be weighing a feature, investigating onboarding failures or deciding whether to invite more customers. Write what you believe now and what could change your mind. Keep the Promise Card in [Tab 01](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1bo9n52j_M4Nx094TObZQVAq1htlB6h9XlySLgFsH710/edit?tab=t.cya3ughhip7h) open.

### Before you begin

1. **Write down the decision.** Be specific. For example, should the primary way people find their documents change?  
2. **State what you believe.** Who needs the result? What are they trying to accomplish? Why do you think your product will help? Separate facts from assumptions.  
3. **Decide what could change your mind.** Identify what you'd need to observe to question your approach. Write it down before collecting feedback.

### During the next conversation or test

**No usable product yet?** Find someone who recently attempted the job and ask them to describe what happened. Follow the sequence of actions before explaining your idea, using [Play 03](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1bo9n52j_M4Nx094TObZQVAq1htlB6h9XlySLgFsH710/edit?tab=t.ds8fxfwg51rl) to investigate the experience.

**Have a working product?** Invite someone qualified to attempt a real task. Watch whether they succeed and how much help they need. [Play 04](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1bo9n52j_M4Nx094TObZQVAq1htlB6h9XlySLgFsH710/edit?tab=t.7dlrt9su90ms) shows how to record the outcome without mistaking your explanation for an observation.

**Already have an early group?** Review their actual results before deciding what to build or whether to expand. Use [Play 05](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1bo9n52j_M4Nx094TObZQVAq1htlB6h9XlySLgFsH710/edit?tab=t.l768kjlu84i5) for an unresolved failure, or [Play 06](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1bo9n52j_M4Nx094TObZQVAq1htlB6h9XlySLgFsH710/edit?tab=t.reojhvytzs5q) when deciding whether the demonstrated value justifies broader access.

### Before you move on

Record what happened, keeping participants' reports separate from your own observations. Write your interpretation and consider at least one other explanation before choosing a next action. You might change the product, continue testing, invite another group, revisit the problem or stop. Whatever you decide, record who owns the next step and what evidence you'll check.

**Done means someone else can understand the evidence behind your decision and know what happens next.**

## A learning cycle from FYI

Here's how I'd describe that early FYI cycle using the six plays. We didn't have this playbook when we built it.

| Part of the cycle | What happened |
| :---- | :---- |
| **Belief** | Finding work documents across services appeared difficult. A unified search might help. |
| **Research** | The survey and interviews revealed tools people used and where their work broke down. |
| **Product test** | Early users tried a search-focused MVP built in five days. |
| **Observation** | Some remembered colleagues or recent activity more readily than search terms. |
| **Alternative explanations** | Search quality, incomplete indexing, or task differences might explain some failures. |
| **Decision** | Explore ways of finding documents through people and activity. |
| **Unknown** | Measured task improvement and retention lift for the original cohort are not established by the surviving records. |

The observation didn't dictate a solution. It gave the team a direction worth testing, with several possible explanations still open. The next question was whether an alternative way of finding documents would actually help someone complete the job more successfully. That's what another learning cycle should answer.

## Keep the learning going

I still use the lesson behind that KISSmetrics diagram. We have more ways to build and measure than we did then. The hard part remains making a sound decision from what we see.

You can use these six plays on a new idea or on a product customers already depend on. Find the real job. Watch what happens. Use the evidence to choose the next change.

**Pick the decision in front of you. Start [there](#how-the-playbook-works).**

# 01  Define the promise

**Start when** You have an idea or need to tighten an existing promise.

**Bring** A possible customer, a recent job episode or an explicit unknown.

**Leave with** A Promise Card and a testable result.

**You're done when** Another person could recognize success and failure without your explanation.

| Before you begin | Bring with you |
| :---- | :---- |
| **Who you're trying to serve** | A working hypothesis is fine |
| **What they do today** | A recent example or a clearly marked unknown |
| **What you intend to improve** | A valuable outcome, not merely engagement |

**Your record** Promise Card

**Exit decision** If you can't describe a real job and alternative, use [Play 03](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1bo9n52j_M4Nx094TObZQVAq1htlB6h9XlySLgFsH710/edit?tab=t.ds8fxfwg51rl) to research. If you can, continue to assembling a qualified group.

## If you're adding a feature to an existing product

For an existing product, begin with the task customers already perform. What do they do now? Where does it fail? How often does it work? A new feature has to improve an outcome that matters to them.

Name the eligible customers, the existing way of doing the job, and what the feature should improve. Record what must not get worse. For an AI feature, that includes correctness and the effort required to check its work.

## Make your first decision in five minutes

In five minutes, write who does the job, how they handle it now and what would be better. Add one observation that could prove your approach wrong. If you haven't heard about a real occurrence, that's your next task.

**Poor answer** “We want people to engage with AI every week.”

**Useful answer, fictional** “A volunteer coordinator needs to fill a cancelled shift before an event. Today they message people individually. We want to test whether one attempt can find and confirm a qualified replacement without founder help. We haven't verified the frequency of this problem.”

**Then** Use the Promise Card below and decide which evidence to collect first.

## Begin with the job

“AI for marketers” doesn't tell you what a person needs to accomplish.

Ask about the last time the job came up. Follow the steps they took and where the work became difficult.

Then decide what your product should improve.

The promise has six parts.

| Part | What you need to know |
| :---- | :---- |
| **Person** | Who does the work? Who else needs to approve it? |
| **Situation** | What triggers the need? |
| **Job** | What result are they trying to achieve? |
| **Existing method** | What do they use today and why? |
| **Better outcome** | What would make their work meaningfully better? |
| **Quality** | What must be true before they could rely on the result? |

You can change your proposed solution as you learn more. The problem itself is also a hypothesis, so keep checking that the job matters.

## See it done with FYI

Here's how I'd fill out the Promise Card using what we learned at FYI.

| Question | Completed answer |
| :---- | :---- |
| **Who** | A knowledge worker who uses documents across several applications |
| **Situation** | Needs an existing document for work |
| **Existing method** | Search different apps, browse folders or ask a colleague |
| **Job** | Find the correct file without opening multiple wrong versions |
| **First solution** | A single search box across connected apps |
| **Testable result** | Person finds the needed document during an authentic task |
| **Serious failure** | They cannot remember enough to produce a useful query |
| **Next action** | Test ways to find documents through people and recent activity |

The search solution was explicitly tested in a five-day MVP. Early users exposed how their memory worked. The team explored other navigation patterns, and the mature FYI interface reflected them.

I can't attribute a measured retention improvement to that change.

[Hiten's FYI product interview](https://www.productboard.com/blog/hiten-shah-age-of-product-excellence/) gives the original account.

## Try the reasoning yourself

Using the FYI example, finish these sentences before reading the answer.

**The original product assumption**

A person can find the needed document if \_\_\_\_\_\_.

**What actual use revealed**

Sometimes the person remembers \_\_\_\_\_\_ instead.

**What the next test should challenge**

We should see whether \_\_\_\_\_\_ helps them complete the same job.

A strong response recognizes that search depends on what the person can recall, while people and recent activity offer other clues. The next test needs an authentic document-finding task.

## Choose the right unit of value

First value depends on who does the work. One person may finish a task alone. A team may need to coordinate. An agent may deliver a useful result while no one has the app open.

Write down where the value actually appears.

**For Beam**, a reasonable first-value candidate is completing an intended task in a remote Mac window. Installing the app does not meet that bar.

**For Slack**, a meaningful test involves a real team communicating through the product. A single employee signing in cannot prove team value.

**For a mobile transit app**, the useful result is reaching the right stop in time to catch a train. Opening the map doesn't prove the trip succeeded.

**For a new AI reply feature in a support tool**, the valuable result is a customer's issue resolved correctly. Accepting a suggested reply doesn't prove that happened.

**For an AI scheduling agent**, a meeting booked with the right people and no conflicts matters more than the number of agent runs.

Choose the measure that reflects the job before you look at the data.

## Copy the Promise Card

`Who is the person or team?`

`What situation triggers the job?`

`Describe the last real occurrence.`

`How did they handle it?`

`What outcome does our product promise?`

`What real task can test that outcome?`

`What failure would make the product untrustworthy?`

`What evidence do we already have?`

`What is still unknown?`

`When is the next review?`

**Weak answer**

Founders need smarter insights, and they should use the product weekly.

The job isn't defined. Neither the value nor the weekly need has been observed.

**Stronger answer**

A store owner wants to know which product page improvement is worth trying. Today they examine separate analytics reports and choose manually. The product should produce a credible recommendation the owner can verify. We still need to learn how often that decision occurs.

This store example is hypothetical.

## Check before you move on

Before moving on, ask a teammate to describe the real task, what success looks like and which result would change your mind.

If you can't name the task, hear another recent example before choosing a metric.

**Next, go to [Play 02](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1bo9n52j_M4Nx094TObZQVAq1htlB6h9XlySLgFsH710/edit?tab=t.lbvo022518zk) and assemble the right group.**

# 02  Assemble the early group

**Start when** You know roughly whose job matters.

**Bring** The job definition, current product readiness and support limits.

**Leave with** Qualification criteria, an honest invitation and an Access Contract.

**You're done when** A real participant understands the arrangement and the team can support their first relevant activity.

| Before you begin | Bring with you |
| :---- | :---- |
| **Job and qualification** | Your Promise Card |
| **Current readiness** | Interview, prototype or usable product |
| **Support and privacy constraints** | What your team can safely promise |

**Your records** Cohort roster and Access Contract

**Exit decision** Start with a group small enough to support honest feedback. Plan who the next group must represent differently before expanding.

## If the participants are already your customers

Invite people who face the job, including some who avoid the relevant part of your product. Power users can reveal advanced problems. Newer and frustrated customers can show you failures loyal users have learned to tolerate.

Use an opt-in preview, a feature flag or a gradual rollout. If teammates share the workflow, consider inviting whole accounts so they see the same version. Track who qualifies, who accepts, who actually sees the feature and who completes the job. Tell participants what may change and how they can leave.

## A practical route to your first five

1\. **Find an existing moment of need.** Review permitted public discussions or your existing opt-in contacts. Record the specific job and recent event, with a source. A relevant participant beats a large undifferentiated list.

2\. **Build a shortlist of ten plausible people.** Include their current method, how you know they face the job, and what would make participation inappropriate. Ten is a working recruiting target, not a conversion benchmark.

3\. **Invite personally.** Ask for a short conversation about the job when no product exists. When the product is usable, describe exactly what they can try and what feedback would help. No automated unsolicited messaging.

4\. **Keep a simple roster.** Track invited → opted in → enabled → attempted → first value separately. Record declines and silence.

5\. **Learn from the first people before widening.** Choose the next participants to challenge one advantage the first group had, such as personal familiarity with the founder.

**Fictional example** A coordinator who replaced a volunteer this week qualifies for an interview. Someone who has never coordinated an event may offer ideas but does not establish the job's current pain.

**Check** Could a participant describe what they get, what you may ask of them, and how they can stop?

## Find people who already do the work

Start where the problem shows up naturally.

That might be X for technical builders, Reddit for hobbyists working on a particular challenge, or LinkedIn for an enterprise workflow. Your existing customers may be the best place to start.

Read what people are already saying about their work. Pay attention to what they tried and which alternatives they trust.

Amy Hoy's [Sales Safari](https://stackingthebricks.com/video-sales-safari-in-action/) teaches this kind of observation. Jason Evanish's [95 ways to find your first customers](https://jasonevanish.com/2013/08/11/95-ways-to-find-your-first-customers-for-customer-development-or-your-first-sale/) is a useful historical collection of recruitment routes.

Platforms change. The important question stays the same. **Where can you find someone who can show you the job today?**

## Select people who match the unfinished product

A useful participant has the job now and works in a setting where the product could help.

A handful of well-matched people is enough to find concrete failures. It won't estimate a market-wide success rate.

Ask people about a recent event, their existing method and any limits that could prevent them from trying something new.

**Example from Beam**

The first public recruiting question asked people to describe their multi-Mac setups. That was more informative than asking strangers whether they wanted a remote-window product.

A suitable first participant would have a task that required interacting with an application on another Mac. Someone running background jobs exclusively through SSH might have a different need.

We then had a real reason to invite relevant people into an early-user group. Replies and group membership weren't proof that the product worked.

[Read the original multi-Mac conversation](https://x.com/hnshah/status/2096383878336303336).

## The invitation should explain the relationship

A good invitation is specific. People should know what they can try and what help you may ask them to provide.

**For research before a product exists**

I saw your description of **\[real situation\]**. We're exploring a better way to **\[job\]**. Could I ask how you handle it now? I'm trying to understand the problem before deciding what to build.

**For a product someone can use**

We're testing an early version of **\[product\]** with people who already **\[job\]**. You'd be able to **\[specific current ability\]**. I'd value watching one real attempt and hearing what gets in your way. Interested?

Make participation optional. Tell people when setup requires permissions or sensitive data.

There's no reason to automatically move someone from Reddit to X or from LinkedIn to Slack. Ask which place works for them.

## Choose the right home for feedback

| Situation | Useful arrangement |
| :---- | :---- |
| **Individuals with the same public workflow** | A small opt-in community or direct message thread |
| **Several people inside one company** | One dedicated Slack Connect channel for that company |
| **Participants who want minimal involvement** | Occasional email or in-product feedback |
| **Pre-product research** | Conversations and follow-up prototypes, without requiring a group |

For company-specific Slack channels, name an owner and define how reports become decisions. Keep customer information inside the company's own private conversation.

**Don't build a community because communities sound valuable.** Build the lightest relationship that helps you understand real work and respond.

## Learn from the first group. Challenge the next one.

Early participants may know you or enjoy unfinished software. That patience makes it easier to find problems.

It can hide problems that a less familiar customer would encounter.

[Karri Saarinen's account of Linear's beta](https://review.firstround.com/linears-path-to-product-market-fit/) describes selecting people whose needs matched the early product, then inviting small groups over time.

A next cohort should have the same important job but fewer advantages. Perhaps they work on a different team, use another sign-in method or don't already know the founder.

[Stewart Butterfield's account of Slack](https://www.fastcompany.com/3041905/slacks-founder-on-how-they-became-a-1-billion-company-in-two-years) describes testing with progressively larger teams. A team product needs to work for a real team, not simply attract individual interest.

**Plan the next group before the current group becomes comfortable.**

## Track who is actually in the group

Keep a roster that shows why each person qualified and whether they actually tried the product. Opting in, installing and completing a task are different events.

`Participant ID (pseudonymous)`

`Job and last qualifying episode`

`How we found them`

`Stage  invited / opted in / enabled / attempted / first value`

`Relevant setup or account constraints`

`Consent and preferred communication`

`Support given so far`

`Next scheduled research or use opportunity`

`Unknown or declined participation`

**Keep the original cohort roster. Record dates and selection rules so you can compare groups.**

## Copy the Access Contract

A sample Access Contract for Beam.

| Question | Example |
| :---- | :---- |
| **Who** | People with actual interactive work across multiple Macs |
| **What they get** | Access to unfinished versions and honest updates |
| **What the team learns** | Whether remote-window tasks work in real setups |
| **What participants may share** | Reproduction steps, safe screenshots and optional retests |
| **Privacy** | No passwords, private files or confidential windows in the group |
| **Leaving** | Anyone can stop participating |

**Your copy**

`Who should participate?`

`What real job qualifies them?`

`What can they try today?`

`What do they receive in return?`

`What might we ask them to show us?`

`What data or permissions might be involved?`

`Where will the conversation happen?`

`Who responds to issues?`

`How can someone leave?`

`Which different people should we invite next?`

**Watch for**

Watch for enthusiastic applicants without the job, or design partners who need a custom service.

Before widening access, check whether the product works without unusual founder help.

# 03  Find the Pattern of Pain

**Start when** You have real participant stories or need to collect them.

**Bring** Recent episodes and how participants were selected.

**Leave with** Episode Records and a provisional Pattern of Pain.

**You're done when** The hypothesis has support, at least one challenge or missing counterexample, and a next test.

**Your records**  Interview Episode Records and Pattern of Pain summary

**Exit decision**  Test one important solution assumption in [Play 04](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1bo9n52j_M4Nx094TObZQVAq1htlB6h9XlySLgFsH710/edit?tab=t.7dlrt9su90ms), or revisit the target job when the evidence is too weak.

## If the pattern is inside an existing product

For an existing product, start with a recent support request, abandoned workflow or failed task. Ask what the customer was trying to do and what happened next. Events can show where a task stopped. They rarely explain why on their own.

Read episodes from customers who requested the feature and those who didn't. Keep examples where the old workflow succeeds. Where you can, record the current completion rate, time or support cost before trying to improve it.

## From a story to a test

**Ask** “Tell me about the last time this came up. What happened first?” Follow the actual sequence, people, workarounds and consequences.

**Record separately** What the participant remembers, what you actually observed and what you infer. A recorded story can be valuable without being perfect recall.

**Compare episodes** Seek a common underlying failure and one counterexample. Do not count several posts repeating one incident as independent experiences.

**Make a choice** State the narrowest possible problem hypothesis and propose a product task that could challenge the proposed solution.

**Fictional example** Two coordinators spent an hour replacing volunteers. A third used an existing group calendar easily. The possible problem is difficult last-minute coordination for some event types. We cannot infer that two-thirds of the market has this problem.

**Check** Could a skeptical person explain what would make your pattern false?

## Get the story before you present a solution

FYI began with research. We asked people what tools they used and which parts of document work caused trouble, then interviewed people whose experiences were relevant.

The useful interviews began with recent events. Those accounts became stronger when we could see an artifact or watch comparable work. In a [2018 Miro interview](https://miro.com/blog/features/hiten-shah-product-development-pitfalls/), I called a recurring struggle among similar people the Pattern of Pain.

Here is a short interview you can use before you have software to test.

| Prompt | What it reveals |
| :---- | :---- |
| **Tell me about the last time you tried to do this** | A real situation and its trigger |
| **Walk me through what happened** | Actual steps and decisions |
| **What did you use, and who helped?** | Existing tools and workarounds |
| **Which part took the most time or went wrong?** | A concrete obstacle |
| **What happened because of that?** | Cost, urgency and emotional stakes |
| **Is there anything important I haven't asked?** | Unexpected context |

Give the person time to tell the story. Avoid describing your proposed product first. Follow up when an action or consequence isn't clear.

**Watch for a Pattern of Pain**

Compare specific episodes from people doing the same job. Keep cases where their current method works, too.

Three people describing a similar problem may give you a reason to test it. It doesn't tell you how common the problem is across a market.

**A real FYI example**

In a later interview, I described someone searching Google Drive for a document, remembering a Slack conversation and eventually asking a coworker while a meeting waited. That gave us a sequence of behavior to investigate. It didn't require the person to predict which future feature they'd want.

[Read the original account](https://www.churn.fm/episode/customer-retention-core).

**Try it on your own product**

`Participant's job and relevant situation`

`The last real episode and when it occurred`

`What triggered the need`

`Actions taken in order`

`Tools and people involved`

`What succeeded and what failed`

`Time, money, effort or other consequences`

`What worked well about the current method`

`Possible common pattern across similar stories`

`An example that contradicts this pattern`

`The smallest product or workflow test worth trying`

Your next step is to turn the most consequential assumption into something people can try. Once you have something to test, continue to [Play 04](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1bo9n52j_M4Nx094TObZQVAq1htlB6h9XlySLgFsH710/edit?tab=t.7dlrt9su90ms).

## Build the pattern from episodes, not votes

After interviews, place comparable experiences side by side.

| Field | Why it matters |
| :---- | :---- |
| **Job and segment** | Keeps unlike situations from being mixed together |
| **Recent episode** | Anchors the story in something that happened |
| **Trigger** | Shows when the problem actually arises |
| **Current method** | Reveals alternatives, including people and manual work |
| **Failure or workaround** | Identifies the obstacle worth improving |
| **Consequence** | Shows whether the problem carries a meaningful cost |
| **Contrary example** | Exposes where the old method works or the pain doesn't appear |
| **Evidence status** | Distinguishes reported stories from directly observed work |

Feature-request counts obscure the work that produced them. Look at episodes, workarounds and consequences before deciding what to test.

**Two different claims must stay separate.**

A pattern is a finding about similar accounts. A prevalence estimate tells you how common something is across a defined population. A selected interview sample usually cannot establish the second.

## A completed pattern record from FYI

Here's how I'd capture a pattern we encountered at FYI.

| Question | Completed example |
| :---- | :---- |
| **Job** | Recover a work document scattered across collaboration tools |
| **Reported episode** | Someone searched Drive, recalled a Slack exchange and asked a coworker |
| **Workaround** | Return to social context when keyword search fails |
| **Consequence** | A work meeting was delayed while the person located the file |
| **Candidate pattern** | People recall who and when more readily than a title or keyword |
| **Rival interpretation** | Index coverage or result quality might also be responsible |
| **Next test** | Give participants real retrieval tasks using search and people/activity views |
| **Missing result** | Original per-person task uplift and repeat value are unknown |

The next product test should challenge the proposed solution directly, rather than assuming the pattern gives us the answer.

## Make the founder's judgment explicit

People may be wrong about why they chose something or how they'll behave later.

Keep your own product hypothesis and seek experiences that could challenge it.

[Keith Rabois's public interview](https://www.lennysnewsletter.com/p/hard-truths-about-building-in-the-ai-era) raises these objections sharply. Returning to recent experiences and actual product use helps us investigate them, while recall bias and selection effects still limit our conclusions.

**Next, watch somebody attempt the real job in [Play 04](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1bo9n52j_M4Nx094TObZQVAq1htlB6h9XlySLgFsH710/edit?tab=t.7dlrt9su90ms).**

# 04  Watch real work

**Start when** The product can support an authentic job attempt.

**Bring** A qualified participant, authorized environment, task and current product version.

**Leave with** An Observation Record.

**You're done when** The result, founder assistance and competing explanation are all visible.

**Your record**  Observation Record

**Exit decision**  Choose an important problem for [Play 05](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1bo9n52j_M4Nx094TObZQVAq1htlB6h9XlySLgFsH710/edit?tab=t.l768kjlu84i5), or continue task testing when the underlying cause remains unclear.

## If you're testing a new feature with current customers

For an existing feature, watch an eligible customer attempt the job with the current workflow and, when safe, with the new one. Record which version they saw, where they went and whether they finished. A customer can have access without noticing the feature. They can open it without getting value.

For a risky change, start with an opt-in preview or a safe test environment. Decide when to roll back. If the feature affects a team, watch how people work across versions.

## A 20-minute task session, when the job permits

**Before** Ask the participant to bring a real task and define acceptable outcome, privacy boundaries and product version. Twenty minutes is a useful session format for a small task, not a universal deadline.

**During** Let the participant attempt the job using their usual environment. Observe actions, failures and workarounds. If you intervene, note what help was given and when.

**After** Record the completed outcome, quality and any failure. Ask what the participant expected and what they would do in the old way. Keep what they said separate from what you saw.

**Then** Identify one important uncertainty for [Play 05](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1bo9n52j_M4Nx094TObZQVAq1htlB6h9XlySLgFsH710/edit?tab=t.l768kjlu84i5). A passed demo or setup step is not proof of a completed real job.

**Check** Can someone else understand what happened from your record without meeting the participant?

## Put the product into a real task

Ask someone to do the job that brought them to your product. Let them try before you explain the interface.

Use their normal environment when it's safe. Ask permission to record or inspect anything personal. Use representative data when the real task could expose sensitive information or create harm.

Let them work as independently as you can. Guiding every click hides what the product can do on its own.

If you help with setup or rescue the task, record it. Assisted and independent success tell you different things.

## A useful task session

You only need six moves.

| Step | What to do |
| :---- | :---- |
| **1** | Ask about the last time the job happened |
| **2** | Find out how they completed it previously |
| **3** | Let them attempt the same kind of job with the product |
| **4** | Note where they hesitate, get stuck or seek help |
| **5** | Check the actual outcome and any serious errors |
| **6** | Ask whether they'd be willing to test a change later |

Don't rush to explain the interface or ask whether they like your proposed features. Watch for the moment they return to their existing method.

A demo can succeed while the customer's job still fails.

## FYI showed us something search couldn't answer

Our first FYI MVP connected document tools through a search box. The underlying problem was finding the right file.

Early tests showed that people often couldn't remember enough to search. They remembered coworkers or recent activity instead.

That observation challenged our proposed interface, while leaving the underlying customer problem worth solving.

The team explored navigation through people and recent work.

[Read Hiten's FYI interview](https://www.productboard.com/blog/hiten-shah-age-of-product-excellence/).

**What remains unknown**

The historical sources don't give us original per-person task success or a measured uplift from the redesign. We should be able to explain the learning without claiming those outcomes.

## A promising detail can hide a serious failure

Suppose a remote-window app feels faster than the old tool, but its pointer occasionally clicks the wrong control. Faster is promising, yet the task may still be impossible to finish. Record both observations.

Speed and reliability both affect the job, though they do so differently.

A faster experience is useful only when people can trust the result. An input error could block the task entirely.

Reproduce the input error in a safe environment, fix it and watch someone try a comparable task. That's stronger evidence than hearing that the new version feels better.

The example is hypothetical. It shows why the actual task outcome matters more than an isolated advantage.

## Observe the right unit of value

For an individual tool, watch someone finish the task without help.

For Slack, look for a real team coordinating work. Individual sign-ins aren't enough.

For an autonomous product, verify the completed action and any harmful side effects. App opens may be irrelevant.

For a mobile app, observe the task where it happens. Timing and connectivity may matter.

For a new feature, record who actually sees it and completes the job. Enabling a feature flag proves neither.

Before recording success, ask **where does the customer receive the promised benefit?**

For a team, individual sign-ins alone aren't enough. With automated work, verify the outcome instead of measuring dashboard visits.

## Write the observation immediately

**An observation from FYI**

During a document-finding task, a person could not supply the information needed for a useful search query. They remembered a colleague connected to the document. We should test whether people-based navigation helps them complete the job. Original task success rates are unknown.

**Now write one from your own session**

`Participant or team identifier:`

`Safe test conditions and consent:`

`Job they were trying to complete:`

`What they used before:`

`Product version:`

`What I saw them do:`

`Where they needed help:`

`Actual result and quality:`

`What the participant said:`

`What I think explains the result:`

`Another plausible explanation:`

`What remains unknown:`

`Next attempt worth observing:`

**Weak observation**

The participant loved the idea and requested folders.

**Stronger observation**

The participant attempted to recover a document but couldn't identify which connected application held it. They opened two wrong results, then asked a coworker for the link.

The second version gives the team a problem it can investigate.

Check your explanation. The participant may have struggled because the product made navigation difficult. They also might have lacked permission to open the correct document. Record both possibilities before choosing a fix. The next test should help distinguish them.

## Before the session ends

Ask what surprised the participant. Explain what you may test next and let them decide whether to return.

Small task tests reveal failures. They don't estimate how often those failures occur across the market.

**Next, take the strongest obstacle to [Play 05](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1bo9n52j_M4Nx094TObZQVAq1htlB6h9XlySLgFsH710/edit?tab=t.l768kjlu84i5) and make a product decision.**

## Put task evidence into your dataset

The observation becomes useful across weeks when it has a stable participant and cohort ID, an actual product version, the definition of the job, an outcome and a source. Record the assistance needed to make the product work.

| Suggested field | Permitted values |
| :---- | :---- |
| **Task result** | Completed, partial, blocked, abandoned, unknown |
| **Assistance** | Unassisted, ordinary product support, founder rescue, unknown |
| **Evidence grade** | Observed, participant reported, inferred |
| **Serious quality failure** | None, unresolved, resolved, not assessed |
| **Follow-up state** | Retest planned, retested, no next opportunity, unknown |

Keep identifiable customer materials private. A future public case atlas should contain only approved anonymous or aggregate evidence.

**Next, use [Play 05](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1bo9n52j_M4Nx094TObZQVAq1htlB6h9XlySLgFsH710/edit?tab=t.l768kjlu84i5) to convert a consequential finding into an experiment.**

# 05  Improve and retest

**Start when** An observation creates a consequential product choice.

**Bring** The job, exact observation, version and candidate explanations.

**Leave with** A Decision Receipt and retest plan.

**You're done when** The team has chosen an action, recorded what it expects and specified what would prove it wrong.

**Your record**  Decision Receipt

**Exit decision**  If the chosen fix solves the target task with acceptable quality, use [Play 06](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1bo9n52j_M4Nx094TObZQVAq1htlB6h9XlySLgFsH710/edit?tab=t.reojhvytzs5q) to examine continuing value and transfer to another cohort. If the fix fails, revisit the interpretation or solution.

## If the decision concerns a feature rollout

For an existing feature, compare the current task with the proposed change. Decide which outcome should improve, what must stay reliable and when to roll back. Use a feature flag or a small release when the risk warrants it. A randomized comparison can help estimate incremental impact when the test is large enough and properly designed.

Track who was assigned the feature, who actually used it and whether the task improved. Extra onboarding or founder help can make a cohort look better than the product really is. Keep the existing workflow available while you learn what the change improves and what it harms.

## The decision belongs to the product team

Record what happened and at least two possible explanations. Consider doing nothing alongside the changes you could make. Write why you chose one option.

Before you ship, write what you expect to improve and what would prove your explanation wrong. Retest the same kind of job after the change.

**Fictional example** Coordinators cannot tell whether a replacement has accepted. The cause might be unclear status or volunteers declining too late. The team chooses to expose explicit confirmation states before adding automated reminders. The test is whether a coordinator can independently confirm a real replacement.

**Check** Does the receipt show why the team made this particular decision and how it will verify the result?

## Turn an observation into a decision

A failed task tells you where to investigate.

The customer may suggest a feature, too. Understand the failure before choosing their proposed fix.

The team has to choose the change. Start with the failed job and the possible causes, then decide which test has the best chance of teaching you something useful.

This continues the practice of regular customer contact developed by researchers such as [Teresa Torres](https://www.producttalk.org/getting-started-with-discovery/). Our focus here is the operating record connecting actual use to the next product decision.

## What if the founder disagrees with the customer?

Disagreement is a reason to inspect the task more closely.

A customer can describe a serious problem while proposing a solution you dislike. Write down the failed task, their suggested change and your own explanation. What would each approach need to accomplish?

The team should choose an experiment that challenges its belief while preserving a deliberate product point of view.

[Keith Rabois's criticism of customer interviews](https://www.lennysnewsletter.com/p/hard-truths-about-building-in-the-ai-era) raises a serious risk. People can be poor judges of their future choices and can misstate why they purchased something. The FYI research approach helps mitigate that risk by asking for past stories and then testing an actual product outcome.

It doesn't eliminate recall bias or guarantee that a few interviews represent a market.

A useful safeguard is to compare what participants say with what they actually do, and record another possible explanation before changing the roadmap.

## Use the Decision Receipt

A receipt should fit on one page. It needs to answer what you thought, what happened and why you chose to respond.

| Field | Question |
| :---- | :---- |
| **Promise** | Which useful outcome were we trying to deliver? |
| **Observation** | What did someone actually attempt? |
| **Possible cause** | What might explain the failure? |
| **Alternatives** | What different responses could we test? |
| **Decision** | What will we change or deliberately leave alone? |
| **Retest** | How would we know the problem improved? |
| **Wider evidence** | Does the fix also help someone less familiar? |

The value of the receipt is that another teammate can challenge the reasoning later.

## See a completed example from FYI

Here's how I'd fill out the Decision Receipt from what happened at FYI.

| Field | Completed answer |
| :---- | :---- |
| **Promise** | Help a worker find the document they need across several apps |
| **Belief** | A single search box is the right primary experience |
| **What happened** | Some people couldn't recall a title or useful search terms |
| **Other explanations** | Incomplete indexing or poor result quality could also contribute |
| **Options** | Improve search, add other recall cues or change the target segment |
| **Decision** | Test navigation through people and recent activity |
| **What later existed** | FYI's mature product included those ways to find documents |
| **Same-user improvement** | Unknown from the surviving evidence |

The direction changed, but I can't attribute a retention improvement to that particular decision.

## Two kinds of improvements worth separating

[Karri Saarinen's account of Linear](https://review.firstround.com/linears-path-to-product-market-fit/) describes **enablers** and **blockers**.

An enabler makes the product more useful for people who already benefit from it.

A blocker prevents another suitable person from getting the value at all.

Linear's early Google-only authentication was a blocker for developers outside Google Workspace.

The distinction helps when deciding what to build next.

| Question | Enabler | Blocker |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **Who benefits?** | Someone already completing the job | Someone qualified but unable to complete it |
| **What would change?** | Depth or quality of the experience | Access, compatibility or a critical part of first use |
| **How would you test it?** | A better task outcome with an existing user | First successful task with a previously blocked user |

**Apply it to Beam**

Better controls for multiple remote windows might enable more sophisticated work. A pointer-mapping bug that prevents accurate clicking may block first value entirely.

I use that distinction to think about what could keep someone from getting value from Beam.

Don't assume blockers always deserve priority. Consider the severity of the job failure and the cost of the proposed fix. Some enablers are essential to reliable core value.

## What to do when people disagree

A feature request is most useful when it comes with a real example.

If two people request opposite behaviors, ask what jobs and environments differ. One may have a good reason to want speed while the other needs safeguards.

Find out whether the requested change would damage an outcome another group depends on.

A serious security, accuracy or privacy issue should take precedence over ordinary feature preference.

**Avoid feature voting as the primary decision method.** Votes measure expressed interest in proposed solutions. They don't necessarily reveal what will make the product valuable.

## Agree on the next decision trigger

Review meaningful results when they arrive. Name the explanation you're testing and who owns the next change. Don't defer a serious failure until the next scheduled meeting.

A short weekly review can handle ordinary results and choose the next test. Urgent reliability and privacy failures need attention when they happen.

## Copy the Decision Receipt

`Decision date and owner:`

`User job and promised result:`

`Person or cohort and product version:`

`Specific task and observed outcome:`

`Why it matters:`

`Other plausible causes:`

`Options considered:`

`Chosen product decision:`

`What we will leave unchanged:`

`What will ship or be tested:`

`How the original failure will be retested:`

`How a fresh user will test it:`

`What is still unknown:`

`Next review date:`

**Weak receipt**

Three people asked for folders, so we added folders.

**Stronger receipt**

Three participants lost track of files after coworkers shared them. We'll test whether a people-based view helps them recover a recently shared document, then compare it with the existing search flow.

The stronger version connects a proposed solution to an observable job.

## Check that the loop really closed

Shipping is the start of the retest.

Invite the original participant to try again and record any extra help or experience they gained. When possible, use a comparable task with someone new.

A successful retest is encouraging. It is not automatically proof the feature caused the improvement.

Send participants a short update explaining what changed and what you're checking. Keep the message focused on the product, and don't expect them to keep working for you indefinitely.

**Next, use [Play 06](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1bo9n52j_M4Nx094TObZQVAq1htlB6h9XlySLgFsH710/edit?tab=t.reojhvytzs5q) to decide whether the resulting value is strong enough to continue or invite more people.**

## Keep a visible decision ledger

When people are helping improve the product over many weeks, the team needs to remember why something changed.

| Field | Record |
| :---- | :---- |
| **Decision ID and date** | A stable reference and decision owner |
| **Person/job affected** | Which part of the product promise is involved |
| **Evidence** | Source-linked episode or task result |
| **Classification** | Enabler, blocker, reliability problem or unknown |
| **Alternatives** | Other plausible ways to improve the job |
| **Chosen action** | What the team actually decided |
| **Shipped version** | What changed and when, if implemented |
| **Retest status** | Planned, completed, failed or unknown |
| **Customer result** | Outcome after the change |
| **Next review** | Owner, date and disconfirming observation |

The ledger is a record of judgment, not a vote for customer feature requests.

[**Play 05**](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1bo9n52j_M4Nx094TObZQVAq1htlB6h9XlySLgFsH710/edit?tab=t.l768kjlu84i5) **is finished only when you know what result you will check next.**

# 06  Prove value and decide

**Start when** You have real attempts or continued-use evidence and must decide who can join next.

**Bring** The original cohort, stage events, quality/support burden and actual job frequency.

**Leave with** A Value and Cohort Review.

**You're done when** One release decision has defensible evidence and a reason it could change.

**Your record**  Value and Cohort Review

**Exit decision**  Make one choice with an owner, review date, and the observation that could change that choice.

## If you're deciding whether to roll out a feature

For a new feature, start with everyone eligible to use it. Then count who received access, who encountered it, who tried the job, who got value and who experienced a serious regression. Keep the dates and versions attached. Clicking a control tells you someone opened it, not whether it helped.

Protect the current product while testing a new feature. Watch task completion, reliability, accessibility, support workload and important business outcomes. A controlled test can help estimate the effect when assignment and analysis are sound. Small handpicked previews are better for finding problems than measuring precise market-wide lift.

Decide whether to keep testing, widen access, revise, pause or stop. Don't expand simply because the early group likes the feature. Look at the work they completed and the damage the change may have caused.

## A release decision should survive skeptical questions

Keep the full invited group visible. Show who was enabled, who attempted the job, who got value and who had another opportunity to use the product. Leave unknown outcomes unknown.

**Fictional example** Four of six people who encountered a subsequent job independently succeeded, from an original invited cohort of twelve. Report **4/6 (66.7%) among observed opportunities** and **4/12 (33.3%) confirmed relative to all invitees**. Neither equals general-market retention. Check support cost and whether a fresh participant can complete the job before widening.

**Choose one** Continue, widen, change, pause or stop. Write the owner, the next event and evidence that could reverse the choice.

**Check** Could someone reconstruct every numerator and denominator and understand the people still missing?

## Judge the product by the job it does

Repeated success matters when the job itself recurs.

Some products serve occasional or one-time needs.

A tax tool may be valuable once a year. An agent may help without being opened. Enterprise adoption may depend on approvals from people who never use the tool directly.

Define successful work before choosing a retention chart.

[Amplitude's work on critical events and usage intervals](https://amplitude.com/books/mastering-retention/your-critical-event-and-product-usage-interval) provides a useful foundation for recurring products. [Reforge's research on infrequent products](https://www.reforge.com/blog/iced-theory-growing-infrequent-products) helps explain why other products need different measures.

## Pick the appropriate proof

| Type of product | What strong evidence looks like | What can mislead you |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **Recurring human workflow** | The job succeeds when it recurs, with acceptable quality and limited help | Logins, retries after errors or founder-prompted tests |
| **Occasional or seasonal** | The important outcome succeeds when the situation actually arises | Treating weeks without visits as churn |
| **Autonomous software** | Verified useful actions, low harmful error rate and continued trust | Number of agent runs or visits to a dashboard |
| **One-time job** | Complete and durable outcome, reproduced for other suitable customers | Expecting the same person to do it twice |
| **B2B company product** | Real user outcome, buyer impact and practical deployment | A happy champion supported by extensive custom work |

Some products fit more than one row. Record separate success criteria for the person doing the work and the organization paying for it.

Also note whether use was voluntary, required by policy or initiated by the product's normal reminders. Those circumstances change what usage tells you.

## Keep the original cohort visible

A useful scorecard shows what happened to everyone you invited, including people whose outcomes you can't observe.

Here's a **fictional** example with a product used roughly once a week.

| Stage | Count |
| :---- | :---- |
| **Relevant people invited** | 12 |
| **Completed setup** | 10 |
| **Attempted a real job** | 9 |
| **Achieved first value** | 7 |
| **Had an observed next-job opportunity** | 6 |
| **Successfully chose the product for that next job** | 4 |

Four of six people with an observed second opportunity succeeded. That's the known result.

Only four of the twelve invitees have confirmed independent repeat value. The others may not have needed the product again, may have encountered a failure or may have chosen another way.

A headline of “67% retained” would conceal too much.

**Show counts and definitions. Keep unknown, failed and not-yet-due outcomes separate.**

With a small selected group, the numbers guide the next investigation. They don't give a precise estimate of market retention.

## Check four dimensions before widening

**Value**

Can the participant finish the promised job? Is the result useful enough to matter?

**Quality**

Does the experience meet the necessary accuracy, reliability, privacy and accessibility bar?

**Independence**

How much founder help or custom engineering does the participant need to get that result?

**Transfer**

Can a new person with the same job succeed, especially if they use a different setup or don't know the team?

You may also need a commercial check. For a product sold to companies, someone must be able to approve, deploy and pay for it.

## Don't confuse progress in one group with readiness for everyone

[Linear's private-beta history](https://review.firstround.com/linears-path-to-product-market-fit/) illustrates why a new cohort matters.

Linear's early users helped improve its core workflow. Sign-in requirements also kept some qualified people out. A different group may expose a problem the first group never faced.

Before inviting more people, find out what could keep the next group from reaching first value.

Slack provides a complementary example. Its preview attracted thousands of requests from companies, while the meaningful product question was whether real teams could work successfully in it.

[Read Stewart Butterfield's account of Slack's early teams](https://www.fastcompany.com/3041905/slacks-founder-on-how-they-became-a-1-billion-company-in-two-years).

An access request shows interest. The next question is whether people can do the job once they're inside.

## Decide at the end of every cycle

| What the evidence suggests | Decision |
| :---- | :---- |
| **The job matters and a key obstacle remains testable** | Continue with a focused change |
| **Current value is dependable and a fresh group can succeed** | Widen to the next suitable cohort |
| **The customer job matters but the interaction fails** | Change the solution |
| **Another identifiable group gets more value** | Change the segment |
| **Users benefit but buying, deployment or economics don't work** | Reconsider the business approach |
| **Serious harm, privacy gaps or missing evidence prevent a fair test** | Pause |
| **The job lacks meaningful demand, risks remain unacceptable or another cycle isn't justified** | Stop |

Don't stay in early access indefinitely because the group is friendly. Set review dates and support limits.

Some products need a different kind of beta. [Jason Fried describes a late-stage beta](https://world.hey.com/jason/a-beta-is-like-inviting-guests-over-a146c056) used shortly before public launch to find rough edges in an almost-finished product. That is a legitimate approach when the core value already works and launch quality is the remaining question.

## Copy the Value Review

`Cohort and selection rules:`

`User job and product promise:`

`Type of value being measured:`

`How many were invited and how many started?`

`How many completed the real job?`

`Did the result meet the quality bar?`

`For recurring work, who had another real need?`

`Who succeeded again, without exceptional founder help?`

`For other products, what outcome proves continuing value?`

`What results remain unknown or unobservable?`

`How much manual support or custom work was required?`

`Did a fresh cohort also succeed?`

`Any serious errors or privacy concerns?`

`Buyer or economic constraints, if relevant:`

`Decision and reason:`

`What would change that decision?`

`Owner and next review date:`

## See a completed decision

Using the fictional twelve-person cohort above, a reasonable decision is **continue with a narrow focus**.

Only nine people attempted the first job, and seven succeeded. Four confirmed repeat success. Before wider rollout, the team needs to understand why setup and first use failed for others. It should also gather better evidence about the missing next-job opportunities.

That decision says what to do next while preserving what we don't know.

**The useful outcome of early access is a better product and an evidence-based decision about what comes next.**

Go to [Tab 07](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1bo9n52j_M4Nx094TObZQVAq1htlB6h9XlySLgFsH710/edit?tab=t.3bzsn4yoxak2) for the complete worksheets and examples.

## The playbook's release gate

The release decision should follow the job and the risks the team can support.

| Question | Evidence before widening |
| :---- | :---- |
| **Does the core job work?** | Actual task completion, measured at the correct unit |
| **Can people trust it?** | Relevant reliability, correctness, security and privacy checks |
| **Can someone new succeed?** | Evidence from an eligible but less familiar participant or team |
| **Can we support the next group?** | Onboarding and founder-help costs are visible |
| **Is the business workable?** | Buyer, permission and payment proof where relevant |

Choose the threshold for this stage before looking at the outcome. If the definition changes, record why.

## The ongoing evidence record

Track participant movement with each stage tied to an event and date.

`Cohort ID / admission date / selection rules`

`Eligible people or accounts invited`

`Accepted and enabled`

`Attempted a real job`

`Achieved first value at acceptable quality`

`Needed unusual founder assistance`

`Had a subsequent legitimate job opportunity`

`Independently achieved value again, if applicable`

`Other verified value mode and outcome`

`Unknown next-opportunity or follow-up state`

`Severe unresolved failures`

`Time and cost to support the cohort`

`Evidence from newly admitted participants`

`Decision, owner and next review date`

Keep quiet participants in the original cohort. A small selected group helps reveal failures, but it can't give precise market-wide rates.

[**Play 06**](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1bo9n52j_M4Nx094TObZQVAq1htlB6h9XlySLgFsH710/edit?tab=t.reojhvytzs5q) **ends with a decision. The next cohort becomes another test of whether the promise holds.**

# 07  Field kit and worked examples

Start with either example. One follows a new scheduling product, and one follows a feature added to an existing analytics product. Then use the five forms on your own work.

## One entire early-access cycle

**Fictional product** A scheduling tool that helps volunteer coordinators find and confirm replacement helpers when someone cancels before an event.

| Play | Decision and record |
| :---- | :---- |
| **01 Define the promise** | A coordinator needs a qualified replacement before an event. Today they use messages and a spreadsheet. The first-value hypothesis is confirming a replacement who actually agrees to show up. |
| **02 Assemble the group** | The founder finds eight coordinators who handled a cancellation recently, invites them to an optional test and records the event type, existing method, communication preferences and access terms. |
| **03 Find the Pattern of Pain** | Three reported episodes involve uncertain confirmation. Two coordinators describe events where a simple group message worked. The pattern hypothesis is unreliable confirmation under time pressure, not a claim about how common the problem is in the market. |
| **04 Watch real work** | Six coordinators attempt real shift-replacement tasks in an authorized test environment. Four reach a verified confirmation with some support. Two cannot tell whether a volunteer has accepted. Outcomes, assistance and product versions are recorded. |
| **05 Improve and retest** | The team considers automated reminders and clearer acceptance status. It chooses explicit acceptance status because the observed failure concerned knowing who had accepted. The founder predicts that a new coordinator can independently verify a replacement. |
| **06 Prove value and decide** | A retest shows one improved task but there is insufficient evidence of natural next-job value or transfer to a fresh group. The team decides to continue testing and admits a small new cohort rather than opening access broadly. |

**Notice how one decision follows from the job through a failure and a retest. Interest and signups aren't substituted for completed work.**

## A complete feature cycle inside an existing product

**Fictional example. An established website analytics product plans to recommend one page improvement a store owner could test. Customers already use its reports to make those decisions.**

[**01 Define the promise**](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1bo9n52j_M4Nx094TObZQVAq1htlB6h9XlySLgFsH710/edit?tab=t.cya3ughhip7h)**.** An owner trying to improve a product page currently reads several reports and chooses an action manually. The proposed feature should help them identify a credible change to test. The first valuable result is a recommendation the owner understands and can verify. The team will also check whether recommendations contain inaccurate evidence or lead to costly mistakes.

[**02 Assemble the group**](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1bo9n52j_M4Nx094TObZQVAq1htlB6h9XlySLgFsH710/edit?tab=t.lbvo022518zk)**.** The team selects eligible existing stores that recently reviewed product-page performance, including newer customers and people who rarely complete the current analysis workflow. A small opt-in cohort receives a clearly described preview. Eligibility, invitation, access, feature exposure and task completion remain separate fields in the roster. The team keeps a way to use the original reports.

[**03 Find the Pattern of Pain**](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1bo9n52j_M4Nx094TObZQVAq1htlB6h9XlySLgFsH710/edit?tab=t.ds8fxfwg51rl)**.** Support conversations and recent task episodes suggest that some owners struggle to decide what to change. Other owners already make decisions easily with existing reports. The team keeps these counterexamples and records a pre-feature baseline rather than assuming every customer needs recommendations.

[**04 Watch real work**](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1bo9n52j_M4Nx094TObZQVAq1htlB6h9XlySLgFsH710/edit?tab=t.7dlrt9su90ms)**.** An owner reviews an actual page and tries to choose a change. The team records whether the owner saw the new recommendation, understood its evidence, found it credible and could make a concrete decision. A participant may open the feature without obtaining a useful result. That distinction appears in the Observation Record.

[**05 Improve and retest**](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1bo9n52j_M4Nx094TObZQVAq1htlB6h9XlySLgFsH710/edit?tab=t.l768kjlu84i5)**.** The preview reveals that a recommendation sometimes lacks the supporting page evidence needed to trust it. The team considers changing the explanation, improving the evidence or narrowing eligible pages. It chooses one response, records an alternative cause and retests with the same type of task. For a sufficiently powered rollout, a randomized comparison with the existing workflow could then estimate the incremental benefit. Until such data exist, the lift is UNKNOWN.

[**06 Prove value and decide**](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1bo9n52j_M4Nx094TObZQVAq1htlB6h9XlySLgFsH710/edit?tab=t.reojhvytzs5q)**.** The team reviews the complete preview cohort, including people who never tried the feature, verified task outcomes, mistaken recommendations, support effort and any decline in the existing workflow. It may widen to a less familiar group, revise the feature or keep it optional. An implemented page improvement and a measured conversion lift are later, stronger evidence than clicking the recommendation. Neither is assumed to have happened in this fictional example.

**An existing product provides a useful baseline. Watch how customers handle the task today, then test whether the new feature improves it without harming what already works.**

## See it done → Try it → Copy it → Check it

**See it done. Read an example and follow the evidence behind its decision.**

**Try it. For the volunteer example, ask what would still fail if acceptance status were perfectly clear.**

**Copy it. Start with the Promise Card. Fill out later forms only after you have the evidence.**

**Check it. Can another person find the source, understand what is unknown and see the next decision?**

## The five core working forms

You can copy these into your notes, a private Google Doc or an AI assistant. Keep private participant information out of public documents.

### 1\. Promise Card

**Use when**

You need to decide what real job your product should improve.

**FYI, written as a Promise Card today**

| Question | Answer |
| :---- | :---- |
| **Person** | A knowledge worker finding a document across several services |
| **Old way** | Search multiple apps, browse folders or ask a colleague |
| **Product hypothesis** | One search box can solve the finding task |
| **Successful outcome** | Correct needed document found during real work |
| **Observation that challenged it** | People couldn't always recall useful search details |
| **Product response** | Explore people and activity as ways to navigate |
| **Remaining unknown** | Original-cohort task improvement and retention |

This is how I'd document what happened at FYI today.

**Copy your own**

`Who is it for?`

`What job are they trying to accomplish?`

`What triggered the last occurrence?`

`What do they do now?`
