`What better outcome are we promising?`

`What task will test it?`

`What failure would make us reconsider?`

`What do we know, and what remains unknown?`

**Check**

Can somebody else run the test without you explaining what success looks like?

### 2\. Access Contract

Use when

You're inviting people to participate before or during an unfinished product release.

**An Access Contract for Beam**

| Question | Answer |
| :---- | :---- |
| **Eligible participants** | People working interactively across two or more Macs |
| **What they receive** | Access to unfinished builds and updates |
| **What the team wants to learn** | Whether remote window interactions work in real environments |
| **Feedback method** | Optional group, direct messages and safe reproduction steps |
| **Privacy expectation** | No passwords or confidential windows in shared messages |
| **Support promise** | Founder triages issues and communicates decisions when possible |
| **Leaving** | Voluntary at any time |

This is an example of how I'd set expectations with Beam participants today.

Copy your own

`Who can participate?`

`What real problem do they already have?`

`What can they use or review today?`

`What should they expect from us?`

`What feedback would be useful?`

`What permissions, recordings or data might be involved?`

`Where and how will we communicate?`

`Who owns the program?`

`How can they leave?`

`What would trigger the next admission round?`

Check

Would a participant understand the product's current limits and what happens to their feedback?

### 3\. Observation Record

Use when

Someone has attempted a meaningful task with the product.

**An observation from FYI**

| Question | Answer |
| :---- | :---- |
| **Task** | Find an existing work document |
| **Existing method** | Multiple search tools and asking collaborators |
| **Attempt** | Use the connected-app search prototype |
| **What went wrong** | Couldn't remember enough to enter a useful search |
| **Reported alternative** | Remembered the person associated with the document |
| **Hypothesis** | Navigation through people might help |
| **Outcome evidence** | Founder-described qualitative test finding |
| **Important unknown** | Frequency of the problem and exact task-success rate |

Copy your own

`Participant ID and relevant job:`

`Product version and date:`

`Consent and safe environment:`

`Real task and expected result:`

`Current alternative:`

`Actual steps and outcome:`

`Where help was needed:`

`What the participant said:`

`What I observed separately:`

`Plausible explanations:`

`Source or safe reproduction link:`

`What we should test next:`

Check

Could a teammate reproduce or investigate the problem from this record?

### 4\. Decision Receipt

Use when

A product team needs to choose which change to make.

**The Linear sign-in decision**

[Karri Saarinen's account of Linear](https://review.firstround.com/linears-path-to-product-market-fit/) describes an early blocker in the sign-in flow.

| Question | Answer |
| :---- | :---- |
| **Customer job** | Manage development issues efficiently |
| **Blocker** | Google-only login excluded some qualified users |
| **What this suggested** | Access restrictions prevented first value |
| **Decision option** | Support more authentication methods |
| **What to verify** | A formerly blocked person can start and perform the job |
| **Unverified outcome** | Measured retention lift caused by one login change |

Here's how I'd record the decision from Linear's public account. The measured effect on retention remains unknown.

Copy your own

`Original belief and product promise:`

`Specific task observation:`

`Possible causes:`

`Alternatives worth considering:`

`Enabler, blocker or another kind of change:`

`Chosen decision and why:`

`Owner and expected version:`

`Original task retest:`

`New participant or environment test:`

`What happened after the change:`

`What remains unknown:`

`Next decision date:`

Check

Does the receipt link a real observation to a decision and a test of its result?

### 5\. Value and Cohort Review

Use when

You need to decide whether to continue, widen access, change direction or stop.

**Completed fictional example**

This example is entirely invented to teach measurement. It isn't data from any of the companies in the playbook.

| Event | People |
| :---- | :---- |
| **Qualified participants invited** | 12 |
| **Completed setup** | 10 |
| **Attempted a real task** | 9 |
| **Achieved the first valuable result** | 7 |
| **Had an observed next opportunity** | 6 |
| **Independently achieved the next result** | 4 |

**What this means**

Among the six observed next opportunities, four succeeded. That confirms independent repeat value for only four of the twelve people originally invited. We don't yet know whether the remaining people had another opportunity.

This suggests that first-use barriers deserve attention. It doesn't justify a market-wide retention claim.

**A reasonable decision**

Continue the early-access program for another focused cycle. Investigate setup and task failures before inviting a much larger group. Clarify what happened for those whose next job couldn't be observed.

Copy your own

`What product promise are we testing?`

`What value mode fits the job?`

`Who qualified for the cohort and why?`

`Invited, enabled, attempted and first-value counts:`

`Quality and severe-failure results:`

`For recurring jobs, observed next opportunities:`

`Independent next-job successes:`

`For other products, verified value outcome:`

`Missing or unknown outcomes:`

`How much founder or custom help was required?`

`Fresh-cohort results:`

`Relevant buyer or deployment constraints:`

`Decision and reason:`

`What evidence would change it?`

`Owner and review date:`

Check

Could a skeptical teammate reconstruct the numbers, see the unknowns and understand the decision?

## Run the playbook with an AI assistant

You can give the playbook to an AI assistant. The assistant should help you apply the method to **your own product**, using your real observations rather than filling gaps with plausible stories.

Start with this prompt.

`Use The Early Access Playbook to coach me through one useful product-learning cycle.`

`My product is [product and current stage].`

`The people I want to serve are [people].`

`The job I believe they have is [job].`

`The real evidence I already have is [links, notes or observations].`

`Begin by drafting a Promise Card. Mark any unverified claims as assumptions.`

`Recommend the next smallest safe research or product test and explain why.`

`After I share the result, help me complete a Decision Receipt.`

`Do not invent customer interviews, usage numbers, outcomes or source links.`

`Choose proof of value that fits the actual job, including non-recurring jobs.`

`Ask only for details that materially affect the next decision.`

`Keep private participant information out of public drafts.`

**What a useful response looks like**

A filled Promise Card, clear unknowns and a specific task to test. After real results are supplied, the assistant should produce a Decision Receipt and a recommendation to continue, widen, change direction, pause or stop.

**What to reject**

An impressive launch plan with no real customer job, simulated feedback presented as research, or a retention target chosen without knowing how often the job occurs.

The prompt above is enough to begin. Use the actual results of your work to complete the next form rather than asking an AI assistant to fill in missing evidence.

## The three historical comparisons worth remembering

**FYI**

We began with research before having a usable product. A focused search MVP challenged our chosen interface and led us to test other ways of finding documents.

**Slack**

A communication product needed real team-level use. Slack exposed the product to progressively larger teams and learned from each wave. Its first-day preview-request count wasn't a retention result.

[Stewart Butterfield's account](https://www.fastcompany.com/3041905/slacks-founder-on-how-they-became-a-1-billion-company-in-two-years).

**Linear**

Its founders selected people with real issue-tracking needs. They stayed close to committed users and learned which improvements helped existing users and which barriers prevented other qualified people from joining.

[Karri Saarinen's account](https://review.firstround.com/linears-path-to-product-market-fit/).

Different companies have different reasons to limit access. What connects these cases is learning from actual work while the product can still change.

## Common objections

Some founders worry that customer interviews produce incremental products and lead teams away from their convictions. It's a reasonable concern.

A story about past work gives us a problem to investigate. A product test tells us whether the proposed solution delivers value. Neither replaces the founder's responsibility for product direction.

| Concern | What the playbook recommends |
| :---- | :---- |
| **Customers cannot predict what they'll want** | Ask for real past episodes, then test actual behavior |
| **Feedback turns into a feature-request backlog** | Find the underlying job and compare different solutions |
| **Three similar stories prove a market** | Treat a pattern as a hypothesis, not a population estimate |
| **Friendly early users distort the result** | Invite another qualified group with different conditions |
| **Research delays the launch** | Time-box the test and end each cycle with a decision |
| **Repeat usage doesn't suit our job** | Define another meaningful outcome instead |

Interviews help us understand what happened in past work. Actual product use shows how a solution performs. Neither establishes the size of the market or replaces judgment about what to build.

## Run your first complete cycle

With an idea, begin with the Promise Card and conversations about real past work. There's no product to observe yet.

With a working product, invite a small qualified group. Watch someone do the job and record the failure that most changes your next decision.

At the next review, decide whether the evidence justifies another test or wider access.

Jobs recur at different rates, sometimes daily and sometimes months apart. Review the next real result and decide what to do.

**If you only complete one form today, start with the Promise Card.**

## Fast self-check before you share a result

• Did we name the actual job and what was observed, not merely an idea?

• Can someone locate the relevant episode, task or product version?

• Have we separated reported stories from observed task outcomes and our interpretation?

• Did we preserve everyone invited, including missing participants?

• Does the Decision Receipt include a second explanation and a falsifier?

• Is the next step a real observation that could change the decision?

**If any answer is no, mark it UNKNOWN and fix the record before treating the conclusion as proven.**

Start with the decision you need to make.

# Resources

In 2017, Marie Prokopets and I let readers follow the research behind what became FYI. We shared the questions we asked and what we learned along the way. Those original emails are here alongside newer work.

I've also included writing from people I've learned from, including some I don't entirely agree with. The collection now reaches into product judgment and AI-assisted development. Find the question you're working through and start there.

# Start here

[**Notes on building products people love when software gets cheap**](https://x.com/hnshah/status/2088663964116983856)

Why cheap implementation makes product judgment more important. I use Meta's habit of studying proven behaviors to explain the learning loop I want teams to develop.

[**The new startup bottleneck**](https://x.com/hnshah/status/2056390241217622502)

Teams can ship a demo and still struggle to say what they learned. This essay asks how a company gets smarter after every release.

[**How to create early access surveys for a new product or feature**](https://producthabits.com/early-access-surveys/)

The survey format I use to find people with a real problem and invite them into further research. It's a useful place to begin.

[**Early access email scripts for a new product or feature**](https://producthabits.com/early-access-emails/)

Actual messages for inviting people to participate before a new product or feature is ready. Adapt them to the relationship you have with your audience.

[**The Product Can Become the Research**](https://www.linkedin.com/pulse/product-can-become-research-hiten-shah-idlyc)

Working software is getting cheaper to make. I explore what changes when you can put something usable in front of people much earlier.

[**The Mom Test**](https://www.momtestbook.com/)

Rob Fitzpatrick explains how to ask about what people already do. A helpful check when you're getting exactly the compliments you hoped for.

[**How Superhuman built an engine to find product-market fit**](https://review.firstround.com/how-superhuman-built-an-engine-to-find-product-market-fit/)

Rahul Vohra explains how Superhuman chose which early users to learn from and used their feedback to improve the product.

# Perspectives worth studying

## Customer development and interviewing

[**The Customer Development Manifesto**](https://steveblank.com/2012/03/29/nail-the-customer-development-manifesto/)

Steve Blank lays out the principles behind testing business assumptions with real people. Worth revisiting when a team becomes too certain of its plan.

[**Demand-Side Sales**](https://www.demandsidesales.com/)

Bob Moesta explains how people decide to change what they're already doing. Especially useful when you understand your features better than the reasons someone might switch.

[**Hard truths about building in the AI era**](https://www.lennysnewsletter.com/p/hard-truths-about-building-in-the-ai-era)

On Lenny's Podcast, Keith Rabois challenges the value of customer interviews for some products. A useful counterpoint to the other approaches in this library.

## Discovery and experiments

[**Opportunity solution trees**](https://www.producttalk.org/opportunity-solution-trees/)

Teresa Torres shows how to connect customer needs to possible product solutions. It gives teams a clearer view of what they're choosing to test.

[**Discovering solutions**](https://www.producttalk.org/discovering-solutions/)

Interviews can reveal opportunities. Assumption tests can tell you whether a proposed solution holds up. Torres explains how the two work together.

[**Why you only need to test with five users**](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/why-you-only-need-to-test-with-5-users/)

Jakob Nielsen makes the case for small usability studies. The five-user guideline concerns usability problems and doesn't establish market demand.

## Product-market fit and AI-era development

[**AI killed the MVP. Long live the IUP**](https://steveblank.com/2026/09/25/ai-killed-the-mvp-long-live-the-iup/)

Steve Blank argues that AI can produce software that looks finished before anyone has tested the important assumptions behind it.

[**Lean LaunchPad, the next generation**](https://steveblank.com/2026/09/30/lean-launchpad-the-next-generation/)

Blank revisits his discovery process for teams that can now produce working software quickly. Useful for deciding what evidence to gather next.

# A note on evidence

These approaches won't always agree. That's useful. A conversation tells you something different from watching someone use the product. Pay attention to what each method can reasonably prove.

The six plays and field kit in this guide remain the working method. I'll keep adding resources that help answer questions along the way.
